sections.text: So far, every program did one thing at a time. A thread lets a program do several things at once. Each thread runs its own code, and the operating system shares the processor between them. thread::spawn starts a new thread. You give it a closure (the code to run, written || { ... }), and it gives back a JoinHandle. Calling join() on the handle waits until that thread has finished.

Threads run at the same time, so if main and the worker both printed while running, the order could change from run to run. Here main waits at join() before it prints again, so the output is always the same. Every example in this unit is built that way: wait for the threads, then print.

join() returns a Result. It is Err if the thread panicked, which is why we call unwrap(). A thread can also hand back a value: whatever the closure returns comes out of join(). Join the threads you care about: when main returns, the whole program ends and any thread still running is stopped.

A thread is like a second worker in the kitchen. The two of you cook at the same time, and join() is you waiting at the door until the other worker says "done". If you never wait, you might finish and leave before they do.

A spawned thread might keep running after the function that started it has returned. So it cannot simply borrow your local variables: they might be gone by then. The compiler checks this for you. The fix is to write move before the closure, which hands the closure ownership of the variables it uses.

Here is the usual pattern: start several threads in a loop, keep the handles in a Vec, then join them in order. Each thread owns its own String because the closure is move. Since we join in the same order we started, the output is always the same.

Sometimes you do want threads to borrow local data. thread::scope makes that safe: every thread started inside the scope is joined before the scope ends, so nothing can outlive the data it borrows. No move is needed. The closure you give scope receives s, the scope handle, and you start threads with s.spawn(...). Whatever that closure returns, here a tuple, is what thread::scope returns.

Coming from Python or Java: Rust threads are real operating-system threads, like a Java platform thread (not a virtual thread), and there is no GIL as in standard CPython builds, so CPU-bound work really runs in parallel. Go's goroutines are lighter, but Rust's std::thread is the closest match to a Java thread. A panic in a spawned thread does not kill main: join() returns Err instead. And data races are caught at compile time, which you will see in the next lessons.

exercise.prompt: Each thread currently returns n. Change the closure so it returns n * n. The program should print: [1, 4, 9]
hints: The closure returns its last expression, and join() hands that value back. Right now the closure returns just n.
The closure is the part after move ||. Its body is just n, so write n * n there. Keep move: each thread needs its own copy of n.

quiz.question: What does handle.join() do?
options: Starts the thread and returns to main right away
Waits for the thread to finish and gives back its result
Stops the thread immediately and discards what it computed

quiz.question: Why does a closure passed to thread::spawn usually need move?
options: The thread may outlive the function, so it must own the data it uses
move copies the data, so the thread runs faster than it would with a plain borrow
Rust only lets threads use data that was copied to the heap first

quiz.question: What is special about thread::scope?
options: It runs the threads one after another, so that they can never overlap in time on any core
It lets threads outlive main, because the scope keeps them alive after it
Its threads can borrow local variables, because all are joined before it ends
